messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 64

Mr. A. is a 78-year-old man who has been married to his wife, Fatima, for 53 years. He sits in the chair across from me with his hands resting on his knees, his back straight, his eyes fixed on a spot on the floor. He speaks slowly, with a slight accent, choosing each word carefully. He is a roofer by trade, or rather he was—he retired at 72, but the work has never really left him.

The story he tells begins in the summer of 1978. He was 32, working on a new high-rise in downtown Los Angeles. It was a job he had done a hundred times before: sweeping the tar, heating the asphalt, laying the felt. That afternoon, the foreman told him to seal a patch near the ventilation shafts. The chemical was a solvent-based primer, strong enough to make his eyes water. He didn’t have a mask—none of the men did. The fumes were thick, clinging to the air like fog. He remembers the taste of it, metallic and sweet, coating his tongue. Within ten minutes, his head was pounding, his vision blurring. He vomited on the roof. The foreman told him to go home. He drove himself, white-knuckled, unable to stop shaking.

That was the first time. But it wasn’t the last. Over the next decade, he worked on dozens of roofs where the same chemicals were used. He learned to ignore the nausea, the dizziness, the burning in his lungs. He told himself it was part of the job. He was a roofer—men didn’t complain. He had a wife and three children to support. So he kept working, his hands black with tar, his skin rough from the wind.

The nightmares started in his late fifties. He wakes up gasping, his throat tight, smelling the sweet chemical even though the room is clean. Fatima has learned not to reach for him in the dark—he flinches, sometimes swats her arm away without meaning to. He avoids the garage where he keeps his old tools. He can’t stand the smell of paint thinner, and he refuses to let anyone use a gas stove if the flame is even a little blue. At family dinners, his grandchildren sit at the other end of the table. He knows they think he is grumpy. He doesn’t correct them.

He retired because his hands started trembling. But the symptoms only got worse. He is hypervigilant—he checks the thermostat three times a day to make sure the gas isn’t leaking. He cannot drive past a construction site without his heart racing. Once, two months ago, he saw a poster for a new housing development and had to pull over. He sat in the car, gripping the steering wheel, waiting for the world to stop spinning. He told Fatima it was a dizzy spell. He does not want to worry her.

His memory has become patchy. He forgets appointments, loses his keys, leaves the kettle on until it boils dry. Fatima writes notes for him on the kitchen counter. He feels stupid. He was a good roofer—he could read a blueprint, estimate a slope, balance on a ridge like it was flat ground. Now he cannot remember the names of his old crewmates. The shame sits in his chest like a second heartbeat.

He has not slept through the night in years. The intrusive images come during the day too: a flash of blue tarpaulin, the hiss of a pressure washer, the taste of metal in his mouth. He thinks he is going crazy. He is here because his son, a nurse practitioner, made the appointment. Mr. A. does not believe talking will help. But he came anyway, because he does not know what else to do. He sits in the chair, and he tells me about the roof.
